summary: Varti are medicated wicks, pessaries or suppositories, made from herbal pastes, powders, honey, ghee or jaggery and shaped for a specific use. Classical Ayurveda uses them in the rectum for constipation and anorectal complaints, in wounds and sinus tracts, in gynaecology and in eye care, always on a doctor's prescription.

body_html:
Long before glycerine suppositories and vaginal pessaries came in neat foil strips from a pharmacy, Ayurvedic physicians were rolling medicines into slender, tapering shapes and placing them exactly where they were needed. The texts call these varti, meaning a wick or a rolled stick. The word covers a surprising range of preparations: a smooth, finger-shaped suppository for stubborn constipation, a thin herbal wick packed into a slow-healing wound, a vaginal pessary for discharge and itching, and the medicated sticks once used to apply collyrium to the eyes or to make medicated smoke.

This page explains the main kinds, the classical background, what research has examined, who should avoid them and how varti are used at Sabka Ved Wellness.

What a Varti is

A varti is made by grinding herbs and other ingredients into a paste, sometimes binding it with honey, jaggery, ghee or cow urine as the text specifies, and shaping it into a wick or cone, which is then dried or used fresh. The shape, length and thickness depend on where it will be used. Sushruta Samhita, for example, describes phala varti for the rectum in terms of size and shape relative to the patient's own finger, so that it is neither too large nor too small.

Main kinds used in practice include:

  • Phala varti or guda varti: rectal suppositories, used for constipation, gas retention and some anorectal conditions.
  • Vrana varti: wicks for wounds, sinuses and fistulous tracts, to cleanse and support healing.
  • Yoni varti: vaginal pessaries, used in gynaecology for discharge, itching and local infection-like complaints.
  • Netra varti: medicated sticks rubbed with water or honey to prepare anjana (collyrium) for the eyes.
  • Dhuma varti: rolled herbal wicks used for dhoomapana, medicated smoke therapy, which has its own page.

Classical background

Varti appear across the classical texts. Charaka Samhita describes phala varti for udavarta (upward movement of vata, with retention of stool and gas) and as an adjunct in basti therapy. Sushruta Samhita, the surgical classic, uses varti extensively in wound management and anorectal diseases, describing how to shape them and when to use them. Gynaecological chapters in Charaka, Sushruta and Ashtanga Hridaya (around 7th century CE) describe yoni varti among local treatments for yonivyapad, disorders of the female reproductive tract. Netra varti are described within eye care.

Varti are therefore a classical, pan-Indian form of medicine, not a modern invention. Today some are manufactured to standard formulations by licensed Ayurvedic pharmacies, while others are prepared fresh in clinics.

How they are understood to work, and what research shows

Classical reasoning

The principle is simple: deliver medicine directly to the site. Rectal varti are thought to stimulate and soften the lower bowel and to correct the downward flow of apana vata. Wound varti carry cleansing and healing herbs into the depth of a wound. Vaginal varti act locally on the tissues and discharge. Each formula is chosen for the dosha involved: astringent and drying for kapha-type discharge and moist wounds, unctuous for dry, vata-type complaints.

Modern evidence

Some varti have been formally studied. A 2016 randomised controlled trial published in Ayu compared Dhatakyadi varti with a standard control in upapluta yonivyapad, vulvovaginitis during pregnancy, and reported it as an effective local treatment in that study. A 2022 randomised controlled trial in the Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine evaluated a Gandhaka Rasayana rectal suppository for postoperative pain after anorectal procedures. In eye care, a 2025 case series examined anjana procedures in refractive errors. These are specific formulations studied in specific settings, often with small samples. They do not mean that any varti works for any problem, and results should not be generalised.

Who may benefit, under prescription

  • Constipation and gas retention, as part of a wider bowel and diet plan
  • Comfort after some anorectal procedures, under the care of the treating surgeon
  • Some vaginal discharge and itching, after a gynaecological examination and appropriate tests
  • Slow-healing wounds and sinus tracts, as part of proper wound care
  • Specific eye conditions, prescribed by a doctor trained in Ayurvedic eye care

Contraindications and cautions

  • Rectal bleeding, severe anal pain, fever with anal swelling or a recent change in bowel habit in adults over 40, which need medical evaluation first
  • Suspected bowel obstruction: severe abdominal pain, vomiting and inability to pass stool or gas is an emergency
  • Pregnancy: vaginal or rectal varti only with explicit approval from the treating obstetrician and Ayurvedic doctor
  • Abnormal vaginal bleeding, foul-smelling discharge with fever, or pelvic pain, until examined
  • Deep, infected or diabetic wounds without proper medical wound care
  • Allergy or irritation to any ingredient

Varti are local medicines, not cures for underlying disease. Do not use them to self-treat persistent symptoms, and continue any medicines your doctors have prescribed.

Varti at Sabka Ved Wellness

Assessment

Dr. Aditya Kunal takes a full history and examines the relevant area. Constipation, for instance, is never treated just with a suppository: he looks at diet, water intake, activity, stress, medicines and digestion, because his focus on gut health means the aim is to restore normal bowel function, not just to force a movement. Gynaecological complaints are approached with dignity and privacy, with your consent explained and asked for at every step, and with referral to a gynaecologist or for tests where needed. You are welcome to bring a family member or companion of your choice.

Preparation and use, for understanding

  1. The doctor selects a classical formulation, either a standardised manufactured varti or one prepared in the clinic.
  2. For rectal or vaginal use, the varti is smeared with ghee or oil for comfort.
  3. It is inserted gently, in privacy, by the doctor or a trained staff member, or you are taught how to do it at home if suitable.
  4. You lie on your side or rest for the time advised.
  5. For wounds, the varti is placed after cleaning and the wound is dressed.

Never make or insert home-made varti; incorrect size, ingredients or hygiene can cause injury and infection.

Aftercare

Follow the diet and toilet habits advised: warm water, fibre from vegetables and whole grains, a little ghee if suitable, and a regular toilet time without straining. For vaginal varti, avoid intercourse during the course if advised, and keep the area clean and dry with plain water.

Why self-treatment is risky

Ready-made suppositories and herbal pessaries are easy to buy online, and it is tempting to try one rather than talk about an embarrassing symptom. The problem is that the same symptom can have very different causes. Constipation can come from diet and habit, but also from thyroid problems, medicines, pelvic floor issues or, less commonly, a growth in the bowel. Vaginal discharge can be normal, or a sign of a yeast infection, bacterial vaginosis, a sexually transmitted infection or a problem with the cervix that needs screening. Treating every case with the same varti can delay the right diagnosis. Seeing a doctor first is not a formality; it is how the varti becomes medicine rather than guesswork.

Why it costs what it does

Most varti are inexpensive medicines. The cost lies mainly in the consultation and examination that decide whether a varti is right, the quality of the formulation, and, where needed, the clinical time for insertion and follow-up. We do not publish fixed prices, but you will be told what your plan includes.

faqs: What is a Varti in Ayurveda?
A varti is a medicated wick, suppository or pessary made from herbal ingredients and shaped for use in the rectum, vagina, wounds, eyes or for medicated smoke.
Is a phala varti the same as a suppository?
Yes, phala varti is the classical Ayurvedic rectal suppository, used mainly for constipation and gas retention.
Some, such as Dhatakyadi varti, have been tested in small trials. They should only be used after a gynaecological examination and on prescription, especially in pregnancy.
Can I use varti for long-term constipation?
Only as part of a plan that corrects diet, water, activity and digestion. Persistent constipation, bleeding or a change in bowel habit needs medical evaluation.
Yes. Examinations and procedures are done in privacy, each step is explained and done only with your consent, and you may bring a companion of your choice.
